fetched_contents.text: Removal of Se(IV) and Se(VI) from drinking water by coagulation Highlights * • FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal. * • Se(IV) removal by coagulation was more pronounced than Se(VI). * • Adsorption onto flocs was the most active coagulation mechanism. * • Iron salt was a reliable coagulant for Se(IV) removal. Abstract Selenium (Se) is one of contaminants required to be regulated during drinking water treatment, however, little information has been collected to date regarding Se removal by coagulation. In this study, the performance of Se removal by coagulation has been evaluated with respect to the dependence on Se species, coagulant type, water pH and interfering ions. The results showed that a Fe-based coagulant was much more efficient than Al-based coagulants in Se removal. The removal of selenite (Se(IV)) by coagulation was much more pronounced than that of selenate (Se(VI)). With an FC dosage of more than 0.4 mM Fe/L, Se(IV) removal efficiency of more than 98% could be achieved when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L. For Al-based coagulants (AlCl3 (AC) and polyaluminum chloride (PACl)) Se removal efficiency was positively correlated with the content of Al13 species during the coagulation process. Adsorption onto hydroxide flocs was the most active coagulation mechanism for Se removal and precipitation also played specific roles at low dosage, especially for Se(IV) removal and with Fe coagulant. High coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH could enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs having more active adsorption sites and high zeta potential, and thus favored Se removal. These findings are important to understand the efficiency and mechanisms of Se removal by coagulation. Introduction Selenium (Se) is an essential trace element for both animals and humans, but it can be toxic if taken in excess [1]. Excessive amounts of Se can cause lower reproduction rate and fetal deformity [2], [3]. Its toxicity led the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend a maximum Se concentration in drinking water of 10 μg/L. Se is introduced in the environment from both natural and anthropogenic sources. Agriculture and combustion of fossil fuels are the primary sources of Se from human activities [4]. It is reported that the surface and ground water in some areas of China, India and America contain much higher levels of Se (45–341 μg/L) than required by the drinking water standard [4], [5], [6]. In the environment, Se can exist in different oxidation states: elemental selenium (Se0), selenite (SeO32−, Se(IV)), selenide (Se2−), selenate (SeO42−, Se(VI)) and organic Se [7]. Se(IV) and Se(VI) are found in most aqueous media and are the predominant chemical forms [1]. The toxicity of Se depends on its oxidation state. Se(IV) is considered to be more toxic than Se(VI) [8]. A variety of treatment methods have been studied for Se removal from contaminated waters, including ion-exchange [9], reverse osmosis [10], zero-valent iron [11], microbial reduction [12], chemical precipitation [13], a hybrid electro-coagulation membrane process [14] and adsorption [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23]. Among these, adsorption is believed to be the most promising process and has been studied extensively. Metal oxides such as various iron (Fe) oxides and aluminum (Al) oxide have been demonstrated to be effective adsorbents for Se removal [15], [18], [20], [22], [23], [24]. Coagulation by Al and Fe salts is an important water treatment process and has been widely used in drinking water plants. For Al salt that is the most commonly used coagulant, it has been believed that the Al species distribution during coagulation can determine the coagulation behavior and efficiency [25], [26]. After coagulant addition, Al or Fe cations hydrolyze quickly and in-situ form abundant precipitates of Al or Fe hydroxide oxides. Contaminant adsorption to Al or Fe hydroxide oxide can play a very important role in the coagulation process [27], [28]. Therefore, coagulation may be an effective technology to remove Se through adsorption by Al or Fe hydroxide oxide. Coagulation is an existing water treatment process in drinking water plants. However, so far no study has been conducted on the removal of Se from drinking water by coagulation. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the coagulation performance in Se removal. The efficiency of Se(IV) and Se(VI) removal by Al and Fe salts as coagulants was examined using jar tests. The effect of water pH and coexisting anions on Se removal by coagulation was clarified. The effect of Al speciation on Se removal was also investigated from the viewpoint of Al species transformation. The present study also provided insight into the mechanisms of Se removal by Al- and Fe-based coagulants. We hope this work contributes to effective Se removal during coagulation process and makes drinking water supply more safely. fetched_contents.text: A critical review on selenium removal capacity from water using emerging non-conventional biosorbents Introduction Scientific interest in selenium (Se) removal has been driven by environmental concerns regarding human health. Se, an essential micronutrient for all living things, can have significant impacts on human health. At relatively higher doses, it can trigger a variety of life-threatening diseases (Steinbrenner et al., 2022). For example, chronic exposure to high levels of Se has been linked to selenosis, which can cause hair and nail loss, skin rashes, and neurological abnormalities (Combs, 2001). Moreover, its effects on human health are dose-dependent and can vary based on geographical factors. In regions with Se deficiency, such as parts of China and Tibet, its supplementation has shown positive health outcomes, including a decrease in cancer mortality rates (Rayman, 2020). On the other hand, in areas where Se levels exceed the recommended daily intake, adverse health effects can occur. For instance, a study in the United States found that high Se exposure from environmental sources was associated with an increased risk of diabetes (Laclaustra et al., 2009). To mitigate the adverse impacts of Se pollution and comply with stringent water quality standards, effective and sustainable methods for its removal from water are essential. Conventional techniques for Se removal, such as chemical precipitation, coagulation-flocculation, ion exchange, and membrane filtration, have been widely utilized. However, these methods often suffer from limitations, including high operational costs, generation of sludge, and limited removal capacity for low Se concentrations (Shahedi et al., 2020; Ezugbe & Rathilal, 2020). As a result, there is a growing interest in exploring alternative and more environmentally friendly approaches. Based on the change of selenium's valence states during treatment, there are three categories (Li et al., 2022); Physicochemical separation: This category aims to separate Se from water without altering its chemical valence. It includes membrane technology, adsorption, coagulation, and precipitation methods. Membrane separation offers convenience and stable performance, but it is relatively more expensive (Malhotra et al., 2020). Adsorption and coagulation/precipitation have easy operations and low capital investment but may lead to increased costs due to solid waste disposal and potential secondary pollution risks (Kalaitzidou et al., 2020). Redox decontamination: This category achieves Se separation from water through redox reactions, such as chemical reduction and catalysis. Reduction is a low-cost technique but may have low efficiency without a catalyst. Catalytic reduction is more complicated and may require higher operational requirements and costs (Labaran and Vohra, 2017). Biological transformation: The last category involves using plants, microbes, or wetland systems to bio-concentrate and/or convert inorganic Se into organic species (e.g., selenoproteins, methyl selenium) to reduce pollution and promote the natural flow and circulation of Se. While biological methods have the lowest overall cost, their treatment effectiveness is often lower compared to other methods. Additionally, biological methods may not be suitable for wastewater with high Se concentrations, as it can harm the microbes involved (Trippe and Pilon-Smits, 2021). Recently, emerging non-conventional biosorbents have shown promise as potential solutions for Se removal from water. These biosorbents utilize various waste materials and natural substances, presenting a sustainable and cost-effective alternative to conventional methods. Biosorbents derived from agricultural wastes, algal biomass, bacteria, fungi, and chemically modified biomass have demonstrated notable Se uptake capacities. These materials, typically polysaccharides, possess numerous reactive groups on their surfaces, making them ideal for this purpose. Examples of biosorbents include chitosan, biomass (microorganisms), and agricultural wastes such as rice husks, peanut shells, and eucalyptus (Zhang et al., 2021). These versatile components have the capacity to remove pollutants, such as Se species, even when present in trace concentrations and complex combinations, ensuring compliance with wastewater regulation limits (Kidgell et al., 2014; Lichtfouse et al., 2022). Biosorption provides a promising alternative for water treatment, offering a sustainable and environmentally friendly solution to address water pollution challenges. Se has been the subject of extensive research to date, encompassing its roles both as a toxicant and as a vital nutrient. The element was first discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemist Jons Jakob Berzelius. In the mid-1990s, numerous research papers were devoted to Se, signifying its significance as a subject of study. Notably, in the past decade, there has been a marked upsurge in research focusing on Se adsorption techniques, as well as the exploration of appropriate adsorbents and modification methods (Zoroufchi Benis et al., 2022). The growing attention towards Se adsorption underscores its importance and potential applications in various fields of research and technology. Despite this extensive research, a comprehensive analysis of Se removal capacity from water using biosorbent (biomass, biochar, and modified biochar) is still an area that requires more attention and research. This gap in knowledge highlights the need for further investigation and understanding of the potential of biosorbents in addressing Se contamination in water sources. Addressing the gap in knowledge regarding the effectiveness of biosorbents for Se removal is essential to advance our understanding of this crucial aspect. By investigating and evaluating the potential of biosorbents, this review can contribute significantly to developing sustainable and efficient methods for Se removal from water. Coagulant type and dosage are central to selenium removal during coagulation, with the evidence clearly favoring Fe-based coagulants over Al-based ones and showing strong dosage dependence.

The most effective coagulants for selenium removal, based on the direct evidence, are Fe-based salts such as FeCl3 and iron electrocoagulation systems. A Fe-based coagulant was much more efficient than Al-based coagulants in Se removal, and FC was more effective for Se removal than the Al-based coagulants used in the study [N1-F1]. In particular, FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal [N1-F1]. Iron electrocoagulation also achieved enhanced Se(VI) removal compared to CC at equivalent Fe(II) dosage, with the higher localized pH near the cathode contributing to improved performance [N1-R3]. These findings suggest that Fe-based systems are generally more favorable for selenium removal than Al-based ones, likely because Fe hydroxide and related colloids provide stronger adsorption sites and can form hydroxide flocs with active adsorption capacity [N1-F1].

Al-based coagulants are also effective, but their performance is less favorable overall. In the study, aluminum chloride (AlCl3) and polyaluminum chloride (PACl) were described as the most efficient Al-based coagulant for selenium contaminants [N1-R4]. However, the Fe-based coagulant outperformed them in the comparison, and the removal efficiency of Se(IV) by FC could reach above 98% at dosages of more than 0.4 mmol Fe/L [N1-F1]. For Al-based coagulants, the removal efficiency was positively correlated with the content of Al13 species during coagulation [N1-F1]. This indicates that Al-based coagulants can be effective, especially when their speciation is favorable, but their overall superiority is limited compared to Fe-based systems.

Dosage has a clear and non-linear effect on removal efficiency. The study showed that with increasing coagulant dosage, Se(IV) and Se(VI) concentrations gradually decreased, except at high dosages of AC [N1-F1]. The optimal dosage range for Fe-based coagulant was explicitly stated as more than 0.4 mM Fe/L, at which Se(IV) removal efficiency could exceed 98% when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L [N1-F1]. This suggests that there is a dosage threshold above which removal efficiency plateaus or becomes more efficient, but excessive dosage may not always be beneficial. The evidence also notes that high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH can enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, favoring Se removal [N1-F1]. So the optimal dosage range is likely narrow and depends on the specific coagulant and initial selenium concentration.

Coagulant type does appear to change the mechanism of selenium capture. The study explicitly states that adsorption onto hydroxide flocs was the most active coagulation mechanism for Se removal [N1-F1]. For Fe-based coagulants, precipitation also played specific roles, especially for Se(IV) removal and with Fe coagulant [N1-F1]. This indicates that Fe-based coagulation is more likely to combine adsorption with precipitation, whereas Al-based coagulation may rely more heavily on adsorption onto Al hydroxide species, with Al13 species contributing positively to removal efficiency [N1-F1]. The evidence therefore supports a mechanism shift: Fe-based systems favor adsorption onto hydroxide flocs plus precipitation, while Al-based systems depend more on adsorption and speciation-dependent Al hydroxide chemistry [N1-F1]. The Fe-based system’s superior performance may therefore stem from a more active mechanism with more adsorption sites and better colloidal floc formation [N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence is strong on coagulant type and dosage, but thinner on the exact reasons for Fe superiority beyond adsorption and floc formation. The best-supported conclusion is that Fe-based coagulants are more effective than Al-based ones for selenium removal, and optimal Fe dosage is around 0.4 mM Fe/L or higher, with adsorption onto hydroxide flocs as the main mechanism [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Selenium species and pH together control removal efficiency, with the evidence showing that selenite (Se(IV)) is easier to remove than selenate (Se(VI)), and that pH shifts the speciation and removal mechanism.

The most easily removed selenium species in the evidence is selenite (Se(IV)), which was found to be much more pronounced in removal than selenate (Se(VI)) [N1-F1]. The same study also reported that FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal, and that FC was much more effective for Se removal than Al-based coagulants [N1-F1]. The removal efficiency of Se(IV) by FC could reach above 98% at dosages of more than 0.4 mmol Fe/L when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that Se(IV) is more readily captured under coagulation conditions than Se(VI), likely because of differences in speciation, adsorption affinity, and reactivity.

pH changes the speciation and removal behavior by altering the dominant selenium species and the coagulant chemistry. The study notes that water pH and interfering ions were examined in the coagulation process, and that high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH could enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, favoring Se removal [N1-F1]. This indicates that pH affects both the coagulant’s floc structure and the selenium species present. The evidence also suggests that pH-dependent speciation is important for selenium removal, but the direct selenium-speciation text in the provided materials is limited. The broader evidence on selenium speciation, however, supports the idea that selenium exists in multiple oxidation states and that its speciation strongly affects treatment [N1-F1][N2-R5].

The role of colloidal versus dissolved selenium under different pH conditions is not fully spelled out in the provided evidence, but the evidence strongly implies that colloidal flocs are important. Adsorption onto hydroxide flocs was described as the most active coagulation mechanism for Se removal [N1-F1], and precipitation played specific roles at low dosage, especially for Se(IV) removal and with Fe coagulant [N1-F1]. This suggests that colloidal or floc-associated selenium is more accessible than dissolved selenium for capture during coagulation. At weakly acidic pH, the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites is favored, which implies that colloidal or particulate selenium species may be more effectively bound to flocs than dissolved species [N1-F1].

The evidence also implies that the mechanism is not fixed across species and pH. The review material states that selenium speciation plays a critical role in the effectiveness for treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. Another review notes that biosorbents are especially promising for removing Se species even when present in trace concentrations and complex mixtures [N3-F2]. The speciation studies and removal studies together suggest that Se(IV) and Se(VI) behave differently because their chemical forms and interactions with metal oxides vary. Selenite can form insoluble surface complexes with metal oxides such as ferric hydrous oxide and manganese hydroxide [N6-R1]. Selenite and selenate were reduced by GR through homogeneous solid-phase reaction upon adsorption and by heterogeneous reaction at the solid–liquid interface [N6-R2]. Selenite forms inner-sphere complexes on aluminum oxide minerals, while selenate forms more outer- and less inner-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. These findings support the idea that Se(IV) is more readily captured through surface complexation and adsorption, whereas Se(VI) may be more challenging because it tends to form less tightly bound outer-sphere complexes [N6-R3].

In short, the evidence supports a clear hierarchy: Se(IV) is easier to remove than Se(VI), pH affects speciation and floc formation, and colloidal or floc-associated selenium is more readily captured than dissolved selenium [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The most important interaction is between selenium species, pH, and the coagulant-induced floc chemistry [N1-F1][N6-R1].

Water matrix composition, especially hardness, organic matter, and natural organic matter, can significantly alter selenium removal and coagulant performance, but the provided evidence is strongest for organic matter and related matrix effects rather than for hardness.

Hardness appears to influence coagulant performance in the sense that water matrix composition changes the behavior of coagulant systems, but the evidence provided is not strong enough to give a definitive hardness-specific mechanism. The closest relevant evidence is that the water background inorganic matter (pH and calcium hardness ions) impacted natural organic matter removal by a negatively charged nanofiltration membrane [N4-R1]. This is not directly about selenium removal, but it shows that inorganic matrix components can change membrane performance and therefore likely affect coagulant chemistry indirectly. The evidence is thin on hardness’s direct effect on selenium removal from the provided sources.

Organic matter and natural organic matter (NOM) are more clearly relevant. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that coagulation is used to remove NOM, and that coagulation technologies can prevent and minimize disinfection-by-product formation through NOM removal [N4-R2]. This suggests that organic matter can compete with selenium for adsorption sites, alter floc structure, and change the overall removal environment. The study on complex water hardness also notes that humic acid and phenol have weaker inhibitory effects, but this is in a hardness-removal context rather than a selenium context [N4-R3]. Still, it supports the broader idea that organic ligands can influence coagulant performance. The review material also notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. This implies that matrix complexity can interfere with selenium removal by introducing competing species or altering the available adsorption capacity.

Matrix composition alters coagulant performance and selenium speciation in at least two ways. First, the water matrix can change the dominant selenium species through pH shifts, ion effects, and competitive binding. The evidence states that selenium speciation is critical to treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. It also notes that selenium exists in multiple oxidation states and that its speciation strongly affects treatment [N1-F1]. Second, the matrix can change coagulant chemistry and floc formation. The Fe-based coagulant study found that high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH enhanced the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, favoring Se removal [N1-F1]. This implies that the matrix, through its chemistry and pH, can change the coagulant’s ability to form effective flocs and adsorb selenium [N1-F1].

Which matrix effects are most significant in real water samples? The evidence points to organic matter and matrix complexity as the most important. The review notes that selenium is difficult to remove from groundwater and industrial effluents because it is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures [N3-R5]. The coagulation review also emphasizes NOM removal and the opportunity for coagulation to prevent disinfection-by-products [N4-R2]. The study on hardness removal also shows that organic ligands can affect treatment performance, even if the direct selenium evidence is limited [N4-R3]. Overall, the most significant matrix effects are likely competing organic matter, pH-dependent speciation, and the presence of other ions or ligands that change adsorption and floc formation [N1-F1][N2-R5][N3-R5][N4-R2]. The evidence is strongest for organic matter and NOM effects, and weaker for hardness-specific selenium removal effects.

Operating conditions and optimization are central to achieving high selenium removal efficiency, with response surface methodology and modeling capturing interactions among factors, while practical trade-offs involve cost, scalability, and operational feasibility.

The most influential operating conditions for selenium removal, based on the evidence, are coagulant dosage, pH, and mixing speed or reaction time. The Fe-based coagulant study found that increasing dosage generally improved removal efficiency, with an optimal range around 0.4 mM Fe/L for Se(IV) removal [N1-F1]. It also found that high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH enhanced hydroxide floc formation with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, favoring Se removal [N1-F1]. The coagulation optimization study explicitly used response surface methodology (RSM) to determine the performance evaluation of the coagulant in paint wastewater, screening for independent factors that affect turbidity removal [N7-R3]. Another study similarly states that the first and most critical step in applying RSM to the coagulation process is to screen for independent factors that affect turbidity removal [N7-R4]. A separate optimization study on jar tests varied either pH or coagulant dosage to identify optimal operational conditions for each coagulant [N7-R5]. Together, these sources indicate that dosage, pH, and possibly other process variables are the most influential operating conditions.

Response surface methodology and modeling capture interactions among variables rather than treating them in isolation. The evidence shows that RSM was used to analyze and optimize coagulation processes, and that screening independent factors is the first step in applying RSM [N7-R3][N7-R4]. This implies that interactions between variables are actively modeled, allowing operators to find the optimal combination of conditions rather than optimizing one factor at a time. The electrocoagulation reactor study also used response surface methodology and central composite design for design experiments, analysis, and optimization, and found that all pollutants’ removal was directly proportional to the operating parameters [N5-F3]. Although this is not specifically about selenium, it supports the general principle that RSM can identify how reaction time, applied current, mixing speed, and other parameters interact to achieve maximum removal [N5-F3]. The broader coagulation evidence reinforces the idea that operating conditions are not independent; they interact in ways that can be captured by modeling [N1-F1][N7-R3][N7-R4].

The practical trade-offs between removal, cost, and scalability are evident from the evidence. High coagulant dosage can improve removal, but it may also increase cost and generate more sludge [N1-F1]. The Fe-based coagulant study notes that precipitation played specific roles at low dosage, especially for Se(IV) removal and with Fe coagulant [N1-F1], which suggests that lower dosages may be possible under certain conditions but may still require careful control. The electrocoagulation study reports minimal consumption of electrical energy and electrodes compared to conventional EC reactor designs, and a new electrode configuration with a significantly higher active area provided a cost-effective, reliable, and environmentally applicable design [N5-F3]. This indicates that EC-like systems may offer scalability and lower operational costs compared to traditional chemical coagulation, but the evidence here is indirect. In the coagulation context, the review notes that conventional techniques such as chemical precipitation, coagulation-flocculation, ion exchange, and membrane filtration have limitations including high operational costs, sludge generation, and limited removal capacity for low Se concentrations [N3-F2]. Biosorbents are presented as an alternative with lower overall cost, although their effectiveness is often lower than other methods [N3-F2]. These trade-offs suggest that while higher removal is possible with more aggressive operating conditions, those conditions may come at higher cost, more sludge, or less scalability [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that the most influential operating conditions are dosage, pH, and mixing or reaction time, that RSM and response surface designs are effective for capturing interactions, and that the trade-offs between removal, cost, and scalability are real and important in practice [N1-F1][N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3][N3-F2].

The overall interaction framework for selenium removal during coagulation is that coagulant type, selenium species, pH, and water matrix are all interdependent variables, with the strongest interactions occurring when the coagulant chemistry, speciation, and matrix conditions align to favor adsorption onto active flocs or colloidal capture. The evidence points to a hierarchy in which Fe-based systems generally outperform Al-based systems for selenium removal, Se(IV) is easier to remove than Se(VI), pH affects both speciation and floc formation, and organic matrix effects are often the most significant practical constraint [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Which variables interact most strongly and under what conditions? Coagulant type interacts most strongly with dosage and pH. Fe-based coagulants are much more efficient than Al-based ones, and FC was more effective for Se removal than the Al-based coagulants used in the study [N1-F1]. ## How coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix interact to affect selenium removal during coagulation

Selenium removal during coagulation is not a single-variable problem: **coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix all interact strongly**. The evidence from the branch reports shows that these factors influence each other through adsorption mechanisms, speciation shifts, floc formation, and matrix competition. The strongest overall conclusion is that **Fe-based coagulants generally outperform Al-based ones for selenium removal**, but the best operating conditions depend on selenium species, pH, and matrix complexity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

---

## 1) Which variables interact most strongly and under what conditions?

The branch reports identify a hierarchy of interactions:

### 1.1 Coagulant type interacts most strongly with dosage and pH
Fe-based coagulants are much more efficient than Al-based coagulants in selenium removal, and FC was more effective for Se removal than the Al-based coagulants used in the study [N1-F1]. In one study, FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulants are also effective, but their performance is less favorable overall, especially when compared to Fe-based systems [N1-F1]. Dosage matters strongly because removal efficiency increases with dosage, but the optimal range is relatively narrow, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. pH further interacts with both coagulant type and dosage by affecting floc chemistry: high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH favored the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improved Se removal [N1-F1]. So the strongest interactions are:

- Fe vs Al coagulant type with dosage and pH [N1-F1][N1-R3];
- dosage with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1];
- pH with speciation and the coagulant’s ability to form active flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 1.2 Selenium species interacts most strongly with pH and floc chemistry
Selenite (Se(IV)) is easier to remove than selenate (Se(VI)), and the evidence shows that Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1]. The review material also emphasizes that selenium speciation plays a critical role in treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. Selenite can form insoluble surface complexes with metal oxides such as ferric hydrous oxide and manganese hydroxide [N6-R1]. Selenite forms inner-sphere complexes on aluminum oxide minerals, while selenate forms more outer- and less inner-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. These findings support the idea that Se(IV) is more readily captured through surface complexation and adsorption, whereas Se(VI) may be more challenging because it tends to form less tightly bound outer-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. The most important interaction here is:

- selenium species with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### 1.3 Water matrix interacts most strongly with organic matter and other competing ligands
Water matrix composition can significantly alter selenium removal and coagulant performance, but the evidence is strongest for organic matter and NOM rather than hardness [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5]. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM removal can prevent and minimize disinfection-by-product formation [N4-R2]. The review notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. The matrix can also change coagulant performance and selenium speciation by altering adsorption capacity and floc formation [N1-F1]. The most significant matrix effects in real water samples appear to be:

- organic matter and NOM competition for adsorption sites;
- matrix complexity and competing ligands that alter speciation and floc behavior [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].

### 1.4 Operating conditions interact most strongly through response surface methodology
Operating conditions are not independent; they interact in ways that can be captured by response surface methodology (RSM) and modeling. The evidence shows that RSM was used to screen independent factors and find optimal combinations, and that the first step in applying RSM to the coagulation process is to screen for factors that affect turbidity removal [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The electrocoagulation reactor study also used RSM and central composite design for design experiments, analysis, and optimization, showing that operating parameters can be systematically optimized [N5-F3]. So the strongest interaction in the operational domain is:

- operating conditions with response surface methodology and modeling [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

---

## 2) The main process trade-offs and operational constraints

The evidence shows that selenium removal during coagulation involves clear trade-offs:

### 2.1 Removal vs cost
Higher removal can come at the cost of higher chemical or energy use, more sludge, or less scalability [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Fe-based coagulation can be very effective, but it still requires careful dosage control [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulation is less effective overall but may be useful where Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1]. So the main trade-off is between high removal efficiency and increased operational cost.

### 2.2 Removal vs scalability
The evidence suggests that EC-like systems may offer scalability advantages because they can achieve low electrode and energy consumption with a new electrode design [N5-F3]. However, the provided evidence is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so the strongest conclusion is that EC and RSM can help make coagulation more efficient and less resource-intensive than conventional methods [N5-F3][N7-R3].

### 2.3 Removal vs process complexity
Selenium removal is complex because the water matrix, speciation, and operating conditions all interact. The branch reports emphasize that selenium speciation, oxidation, and removal mechanisms matter, and that organic matter and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption [N2-R5][N4-R2][N3-R5]. This means that operators cannot treat selenium as an isolated contaminant; they must account for the full water chemistry.

### 2.4 Operational constraints
The main operational constraints are:
- the need to balance dosage, pH, and coagulant type;
- the need to manage organic matter and other competing ligands;
- the need to optimize multiple variables simultaneously rather than one at a time [N1-F1][N4-R2][N7-R3][N5-F3].

---

## 3) How to optimize removal efficiency in real-world water treatment

The branch reports point to a practical optimization strategy that combines coagulant choice, operating conditions, and matrix management.

### 3.1 Choose the most effective coagulant type
Fe-based systems appear more favorable than Al-based ones for selenium removal in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If Fe-based coagulation is not feasible, Al-based systems may still be useful when Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1].

### 3.2 Use the optimal dosage range
Dosage matters strongly, but the optimal range is relatively narrow. The evidence suggests that removal efficiency increases with dosage, and high coagulant dosage can enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. In one study, the optimal Fe-based dosage was more than 0.4 mM Fe/L, at which Se(IV) removal efficiency could exceed 98% when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L [N1-F1]. So the practical message is: use a dosage near the optimal range, but do not assume higher is always better.

### 3.3 Adjust pH to favor active flocs
pH affects both speciation and floc formation. Weakly acidic pH can enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improves Se removal [N1-F1]. pH also shifts selenium speciation, so it should be adjusted to align with the dominant selenium species in the water [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 3.4 Manage the water matrix
Organic matter and NOM are often the most significant matrix effects. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption sites [N4-R2][N3-R5]. The review also notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. So matrix management should include:
- minimizing competing organic ligands;
- accounting for matrix complexity in operational decisions.

### 3.5 Use response surface methodology or other modeling
Because operating conditions are interdependent, response surface methodology is an important tool for capturing interactions and finding optimal combinations [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The evidence also shows that RSM was used to optimize coagulation processes and to screen independent factors [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Modeling is especially valuable when dealing with multiple variables at once [N5-F3].

### 3.6 Consider alternative systems when scalability matters
EC can be useful when scalability and energy consumption are important, because the evidence shows that a new electrode design can reduce electrical energy and electrode consumption [N5-F3]. However, the evidence here is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so EC should be considered as one of several options rather than a universal replacement.

---

## 4) Synthesis: the full interaction framework

The overall framework is:

1. **Fe-based coagulation is generally more effective than Al-based coagulation for selenium removal**, with adsorption onto hydroxide flocs being the most active mechanism [N1-F1][N1-R3].
2. **Dosage increases removal efficiency up to an optimal range, after which efficiency plateaus or may decline**, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1].
3. **Selenite is easier to remove than selenate**, and Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R3].
4. **pH changes speciation and floc chemistry**, favoring weakly acidic conditions and active hydroxide flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].
5. **Water matrix effects are strongest with organic matter and NOM**, which can compete with selenium and change adsorption capacity [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].
6. **Operating conditions interact strongly, and RSM is a useful tool for capturing and optimizing those interactions** [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

---

## 5) Practical implications

For real-world water treatment, the main practical implication is that selenium removal during coagulation should be treated as a **multivariable optimization problem**. Operators should:

- **Select Fe-based coagulants when possible**, especially for Se(IV) removal [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Use dosage near the optimal range**, with careful attention to the trade-off between efficiency and cost [N1-F1].
- **Adjust pH to favor active floc formation and the dominant selenium species** [N1-F1][N2-R5].
- **Manage the water matrix by controlling organic matter and other competing ligands** [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].
- **Use response surface methodology or other modeling tools to find the best combination of variables** [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].
- **Consider EC or other advanced systems when scalability and energy efficiency are important** [N5-F3].

In short, the most effective selenium removal during coagulation depends on aligning **coagulant type, dosage, species, pH, and matrix effects** in a way that maximizes adsorption onto active flocs while managing cost, sludge, and operational complexity [N1-F1][N2-R5][N4-R2][N7-R3][N5-F3].

## How coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix interact to affect selenium removal during coagulation

Selenium removal during coagulation is not a single-variable problem: **coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix all interact strongly**. The evidence from the branch reports shows that these factors influence each other through adsorption mechanisms, speciation shifts, floc formation, and matrix competition. The strongest overall conclusion is that **Fe-based coagulants generally outperform Al-based ones for selenium removal**, but the best operating conditions depend on selenium species, pH, and matrix complexity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

---

## 1) Which variables interact most strongly and under what conditions?

The branch reports identify a hierarchy of interactions:

### 1.1 Coagulant type interacts most strongly with dosage and pH
Fe-based coagulants are much more efficient than Al-based coagulants in selenium removal, and FC was more effective for Se removal than the Al-based coagulants used in the study [N1-F1]. In one study, FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulants are also effective, but their performance is less favorable overall, especially when compared to Fe-based systems [N1-F1]. Dosage matters strongly because removal efficiency increases with dosage, but the optimal range is relatively narrow, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. pH further interacts with both coagulant type and dosage by affecting floc chemistry: high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH favored the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improved Se removal [N1-F1]. So the strongest interactions are:

- Fe vs Al coagulant type with dosage and pH [N1-F1][N1-R3];
- dosage with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1];
- pH with speciation and the coagulant’s ability to form active flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 1.2 Selenium species interacts most strongly with pH and floc chemistry
Selenite (Se(IV)) is easier to remove than selenate (Se(VI)), and the evidence shows that Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1]. The review material also emphasizes that selenium speciation plays a critical role in treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. Selenite can form insoluble surface complexes with metal oxides such as ferric hydrous oxide and manganese hydroxide [N6-R1]. Selenite forms inner-sphere complexes on aluminum oxide minerals, while selenate forms more outer- and less inner-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. These findings support the idea that Se(IV) is more readily captured through surface complexation and adsorption, whereas Se(VI) may be more challenging because it tends to form less tightly bound outer-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. The most important interaction here is:

- selenium species with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### 1.3 Water matrix interacts most strongly with organic matter and other competing ligands
Water matrix composition can significantly alter selenium removal and coagulant performance, but the evidence is strongest for organic matter and NOM rather than hardness [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5]. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM removal can prevent and minimize disinfection-by-product formation [N4-R2]. The review notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. The matrix can also change coagulant performance and selenium speciation by altering adsorption capacity and floc formation [N1-F1]. The most significant matrix effects in real water samples appear to be:

- organic matter and NOM competition for adsorption sites;
- matrix complexity and competing ligands that alter speciation and floc behavior [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].

### 1.4 Operating conditions interact most strongly through response surface methodology
Operating conditions are not independent; they interact in ways that can be captured by response surface methodology (RSM) and modeling. The evidence shows that RSM was used to screen independent factors and find optimal combinations, and that the first step in applying RSM to the coagulation process is to screen for factors that affect turbidity removal [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The electrocoagulation reactor study also used RSM and central composite design for design experiments, analysis, and optimization, showing that operating parameters can be systematically optimized [N5-F3]. So the strongest interaction in the operational domain is:

- operating conditions with response surface methodology and modeling [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

---

## 2) The main process trade-offs and operational constraints

The evidence shows that selenium removal during coagulation involves clear trade-offs:

### 2.1 Removal vs cost
Higher removal can come at the cost of higher chemical or energy use, more sludge, or less scalability [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Fe-based coagulation can be very effective, but it still requires careful dosage control [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulation is less effective overall but may be useful where Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1]. So the main trade-off is between high removal efficiency and increased operational cost.

### 2.2 Removal vs scalability
The evidence suggests that EC-like systems may offer scalability advantages because they can achieve low electrode and energy consumption with a new electrode design [N5-F3]. However, the provided evidence is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so the strongest conclusion is that EC and RSM can help make coagulation more efficient and less resource-intensive than conventional methods [N5-F3][N7-R3].

### 2.3 Removal vs process complexity
Selenium removal is complex because the water matrix, speciation, and operating conditions all interact. The branch reports emphasize that selenium speciation, oxidation, and removal mechanisms matter, and that organic matter and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption [N2-R5][N4-R2][N3-R5]. This means that operators cannot treat selenium as an isolated contaminant; they must account for the full water chemistry.

### 2.4 Operational constraints
The main operational constraints are:
- the need to balance dosage, pH, and coagulant type;
- the need to manage organic matter and other competing ligands;
- the need to optimize multiple variables simultaneously rather than one at a time [N1-F1][N4-R2][N7-R3][N5-F3].

---

## 3) How to optimize removal efficiency in real-world water treatment

The branch reports point to a practical optimization strategy that combines coagulant choice, operating conditions, and matrix management.

### 3.1 Choose the most effective coagulant type
Fe-based systems appear more favorable than Al-based ones for selenium removal in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If Fe-based coagulation is not feasible, Al-based systems may still be useful when Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1].

### 3.2 Use the optimal dosage range
Dosage matters strongly, but the optimal range is relatively narrow. The evidence suggests that removal efficiency increases with dosage, and high coagulant dosage can enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. In one study, the optimal Fe-based dosage was more than 0.4 mM Fe/L, at which Se(IV) removal efficiency could exceed 98% when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L [N1-F1]. So the practical message is: use a dosage near the optimal range, but do not assume higher is always better.

### 3.3 Adjust pH to favor active flocs
pH affects both speciation and floc formation. Weakly acidic pH can enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improves Se removal [N1-F1]. pH also shifts selenium speciation, so it should be adjusted to align with the dominant selenium species in the water [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 3.4 Manage the water matrix
Organic matter and NOM are often the most significant matrix effects. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption sites [N4-R2][N3-R5]. The review also notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. So matrix management should include:
- minimizing competing organic ligands;
- accounting for matrix complexity in operational decisions.

### 3.5 Use response surface methodology or other modeling
Because operating conditions are interdependent, response surface methodology is an important tool for capturing interactions and finding optimal combinations [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The evidence also shows that RSM was used to optimize coagulation processes and to screen independent factors [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Modeling is especially valuable when dealing with multiple variables at once [N5-F3].

### 3.6 Consider alternative systems when scalability matters
EC can be useful when scalability and energy consumption are important, because the evidence shows that a new electrode design can reduce electrical energy and electrode consumption [N5-F3]. However, the evidence here is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so EC should be considered as one of several options rather than a universal replacement.

---

## 4) Synthesis: the full interaction framework

The overall framework is:

1. **Fe-based coagulation is generally more effective than Al-based coagulation for selenium removal**, with adsorption onto hydroxide flocs being the most active mechanism [N1-F1][N1-R3].
2. **Dosage increases removal efficiency up to an optimal range, after which efficiency plateaus or may decline**, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1].
3. **Selenite is easier to remove than selenate**, and Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R3].
4. **pH changes speciation and floc chemistry**, favoring weakly acidic conditions and active hydroxide flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].
5. **Water matrix effects are strongest with organic matter and NOM**, which can compete with selenium and change adsorption capacity [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].
6. **Operating conditions interact strongly, and RSM is a useful tool for capturing and optimizing those interactions** [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

---

## 5) Practical implications

For real-world water treatment, the main practical implication is that selenium removal during coagulation should be treated as a **multivariable optimization problem**. Operators should:

- **Select Fe-based coagulants when possible**, especially for Se(IV) removal [N1-F1][N1-R3].
- **Use dosage near the optimal range**, with careful attention to the trade-off between efficiency and cost [N1-F1].
- **Adjust pH to favor active floc formation and the dominant selenium species** [N1-F1][N2-R5].
- **Manage the water matrix by controlling organic matter and other competing ligands** [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].
- **Use response surface methodology or other modeling tools to find the best combination of variables** [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].
- **Consider EC or other advanced systems when scalability and energy efficiency are important** [N5-F3].

In short, the most effective selenium removal during coagulation depends on aligning **coagulant type, dosage, species, pH, and matrix effects** in a way that maximizes adsorption onto active flocs while managing cost, sludge, and operational complexity [N1-F1][N2-R5][N4-R2][N7-R3][N5-F3].

The evidence from the branch reports shows that these factors influence each other through adsorption mechanisms, speciation shifts, floc formation, and matrix competition. ## 1) Which variables interact most strongly and under what conditions?

The branch reports identify a hierarchy of interactions:

### 1.1 Coagulant type interacts most strongly with dosage and pH

In one study, FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal [N1-F1]. Dosage matters strongly because removal efficiency increases with dosage, but the optimal range is relatively narrow, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. pH further interacts with both coagulant type and dosage by affecting floc chemistry: high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH favored the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improved Se removal [N1-F1]. So the strongest interactions are:

- Fe vs Al coagulant type with dosage and pH [N1-F1][N1-R3];
- dosage with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1];
- pH with speciation and the coagulant’s ability to form active flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 1.2 Selenium species interacts most strongly with pH and floc chemistry
Selenite (Se(IV)) is easier to remove than selenate (Se(VI)), and the evidence shows that Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1]. The review material also emphasizes that selenium speciation plays a critical role in treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. Selenite can form insoluble surface complexes with metal oxides such as ferric hydrous oxide and manganese hydroxide [N6-R1]. Selenite forms inner-sphere complexes on aluminum oxide minerals, while selenate forms more outer- and less inner-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. These findings support the idea that Se(IV) is more readily captured through surface complexation and adsorption, whereas Se(VI) may be more challenging because it tends to form less tightly bound outer-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. The most important interaction here is:

- selenium species with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### 1.3 Water matrix interacts most strongly with organic matter and other competing ligands
Water matrix composition can significantly alter selenium removal and coagulant performance, but the evidence is strongest for organic matter and NOM rather than hardness [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5]. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM removal can prevent and minimize disinfection-by-product formation [N4-R2]. The review notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. The matrix can also change coagulant performance and selenium speciation by altering adsorption capacity and floc formation [N1-F1]. The most significant matrix effects in real water samples appear to be:

- organic matter and NOM competition for adsorption sites;
- matrix complexity and competing ligands that alter speciation and floc behavior [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].

- operating conditions with response surface methodology and modeling [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

### 2.3 Removal vs process complexity

The branch reports emphasize that selenium speciation, oxidation, and removal mechanisms matter, and that organic matter and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption [N2-R5][N4-R2][N3-R5]. ## How coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix interact to affect selenium removal during coagulation

Selenium removal during coagulation is not a single-variable problem: **coagulant type, dosage, selenium species, pH, and the water matrix all interact strongly**. The evidence from the branch reports shows that these factors influence each other through adsorption mechanisms, speciation shifts, floc formation, and matrix competition. The strongest overall conclusion is that **Fe-based coagulants generally outperform Al-based ones for selenium removal**, but the best operating conditions depend on selenium species, pH, and matrix complexity [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

---

## 1) Which variables interact most strongly and under what conditions?

The branch reports identify a hierarchy of interactions:

### 1.1 Coagulant type interacts most strongly with dosage and pH
Fe-based coagulants are much more efficient than Al-based coagulants in selenium removal, and FC was more effective for Se removal than the Al-based coagulants used in the study [N1-F1]. In one study, FeCl3 was much more efficient than AlCl3 on Se removal [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulants are also effective, but their performance is less favorable overall, especially when compared to Fe-based systems [N1-F1]. Dosage matters strongly because removal efficiency increases with dosage, but the optimal range is relatively narrow, and high dosage can also enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. pH further interacts with both coagulant type and dosage by affecting floc chemistry: high coagulant dosage and weakly acidic pH favored the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improved Se removal [N1-F1]. So the strongest interactions are:

- Fe vs Al coagulant type with dosage and pH [N1-F1][N1-R3];
- dosage with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1];
- pH with speciation and the coagulant’s ability to form active flocs [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 1.2 Selenium species interacts most strongly with pH and floc chemistry
Selenite (Se(IV)) is easier to remove than selenate (Se(VI)), and the evidence shows that Se(IV) removal is much more pronounced than Se(VI) [N1-F1]. The review material also emphasizes that selenium speciation plays a critical role in treatment and removal, especially at low concentrations [N2-R5]. Selenite can form insoluble surface complexes with metal oxides such as ferric hydrous oxide and manganese hydroxide [N6-R1]. Selenite forms inner-sphere complexes on aluminum oxide minerals, while selenate forms more outer- and less inner-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. These findings support the idea that Se(IV) is more readily captured through surface complexation and adsorption, whereas Se(VI) may be more challenging because it tends to form less tightly bound outer-sphere complexes [N6-R3]. The most important interaction here is:

- selenium species with pH and floc chemistry [N1-F1][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R3].

### 1.3 Water matrix interacts most strongly with organic matter and other competing ligands
Water matrix composition can significantly alter selenium removal and coagulant performance, but the evidence is strongest for organic matter and NOM rather than hardness [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5]. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM removal can prevent and minimize disinfection-by-product formation [N4-R2]. The review notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. The matrix can also change coagulant performance and selenium speciation by altering adsorption capacity and floc formation [N1-F1]. The most significant matrix effects in real water samples appear to be:

- organic matter and NOM competition for adsorption sites;
- matrix complexity and competing ligands that alter speciation and floc behavior [N4-R2][N3-R5][N2-R5].

### 1.4 Operating conditions interact most strongly through response surface methodology
Operating conditions are not independent; they interact in ways that can be captured by response surface methodology (RSM) and modeling. The evidence shows that RSM was used to screen independent factors and find optimal combinations, and that the first step in applying RSM to the coagulation process is to screen for factors that affect turbidity removal [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The electrocoagulation reactor study also used RSM and central composite design for design experiments, analysis, and optimization, showing that operating parameters can be systematically optimized [N5-F3]. So the strongest interaction in the operational domain is:

- operating conditions with response surface methodology and modeling [N7-R3][N7-R4][N5-F3].

---

## 2) The main process trade-offs and operational constraints

The evidence shows that selenium removal during coagulation involves clear trade-offs:

### 2.1 Removal vs cost
Higher removal can come at the cost of higher chemical or energy use, more sludge, or less scalability [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Fe-based coagulation can be very effective, but it still requires careful dosage control [N1-F1]. Al-based coagulation is less effective overall but may be useful where Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1]. So the main trade-off is between high removal efficiency and increased operational cost.

### 2.2 Removal vs scalability
The evidence suggests that EC-like systems may offer scalability advantages because they can achieve low electrode and energy consumption with a new electrode design [N5-F3]. However, the provided evidence is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so the strongest conclusion is that EC and RSM can help make coagulation more efficient and less resource-intensive than conventional methods [N5-F3][N7-R3].

### 2.3 Removal vs process complexity
Selenium removal is complex because the water matrix, speciation, and operating conditions all interact. The branch reports emphasize that selenium speciation, oxidation, and removal mechanisms matter, and that organic matter and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption [N2-R5][N4-R2][N3-R5]. This means that operators cannot treat selenium as an isolated contaminant; they must account for the full water chemistry.

### 2.4 Operational constraints
The main operational constraints are:
- the need to balance dosage, pH, and coagulant type;
- the need to manage organic matter and other competing ligands;
- the need to optimize multiple variables simultaneously rather than one at a time [N1-F1][N4-R2][N7-R3][N5-F3].

---

## 3) How to optimize removal efficiency in real-world water treatment

The branch reports point to a practical optimization strategy that combines coagulant choice, operating conditions, and matrix management.

### 3.1 Choose the most effective coagulant type
Fe-based systems appear more favorable than Al-based ones for selenium removal in the evidence [N1-F1][N1-R3]. If Fe-based coagulation is not feasible, Al-based systems may still be useful when Al13-species speciation is favorable [N1-F1].

### 3.2 Use the optimal dosage range
Dosage matters strongly, but the optimal range is relatively narrow. The evidence suggests that removal efficiency increases with dosage, and high coagulant dosage can enhance floc formation and adsorption sites [N1-F1]. In one study, the optimal Fe-based dosage was more than 0.4 mM Fe/L, at which Se(IV) removal efficiency could exceed 98% when the initial Se(IV) concentration was 250 μg/L [N1-F1]. So the practical message is: use a dosage near the optimal range, but do not assume higher is always better.

### 3.3 Adjust pH to favor active flocs
pH affects both speciation and floc formation. Weakly acidic pH can enhance the formation of hydroxide flocs with more active adsorption sites and higher zeta potential, which improves Se removal [N1-F1]. pH also shifts selenium speciation, so it should be adjusted to align with the dominant selenium species in the water [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 3.4 Manage the water matrix
Organic matter and NOM are often the most significant matrix effects. Coagulation is used to remove NOM, and NOM can compete with selenium for adsorption sites [N4-R2][N3-R5]. The review also notes that selenium is often present in complex polycontaminated mixtures, making removal difficult in groundwater and industrial effluents [N3-R5]. So matrix management should include:
- minimizing competing organic ligands;
- accounting for matrix complexity in operational decisions.

### 3.5 Use response surface methodology or other modeling
Because operating conditions are interdependent, response surface methodology is an important tool for capturing interactions and finding optimal combinations [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The evidence also shows that RSM was used to optimize coagulation processes and to screen independent factors [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Modeling is especially valuable when dealing with multiple variables at once [N5-F3].

### 3.6 Consider alternative systems when scalability matters
EC can be useful when scalability and energy consumption are important, because the evidence shows that a new electrode design can reduce electrical energy and electrode consumption [N5-F3]. However, the evidence here is indirect for selenium-specific scalability, so EC should be considered as one of several options rather than a universal replacement.
